..
Issued at 245 PM CDT Mon Aug 31 2026

Sunny and warm conditions persist this afternoon as temperatures 
have warmed to 80s. With a cold front now southeast of the area, dew 
points have lowered to 50s and 60s. Still seeing heat indices up to 
80s to low 90s, so some humid conditions remain though not as humid 
as what we saw this weekend. A weak low level jet (LLJ) is expected 
to develop tonight which will develop showers and potentially an 
isolated thunderstorm across Nebraska. These showers will push 
east/northeastwards into a worsening environment. They could still 
be capable of lightning though not expected to be strong nor severe. 
Low temperatures will remain quite mild overnight, with lows only 
falling to the 60s. 

The showers will push through the area during the morning to early 
afternoon hours. This will leave the rest of the afternoon on the 
dry side of things. With some cloud cover remaining aloft, highs 
look to remain warm but be slightly cooler than Monday's highs with 
temperatures in the 80s up to about 90F. Chances for severe storms 
begin to increase after 6 pm as a shortwave trough ejects out of the 
Rockies and into the Northern Plains. The previously mentioned front 
will begin to return northwards as a warm front due to the mass 
response from the wave. A sufficient warm sector will be in place 
ahead of the boundary with dew points in the 60s to 70s. Some 
capping will be in place which may limit the extent of convection 
early on. Latest hi-res guidance continues to show moderate variance 
but is beginning to show a consensus of storms developing across 
central and north central Nebraska and possibly south central South 
Dakota. These showers and storms will push into the area during the 
evening timeframe but the remaining uncertainty revolves around 
storm mode. Think a custer of storms is possible with embedded multi-
cells to even supercells. As the storms push further into the 
forecast area, they will become more elevated due to increased 
capping over the area. Storm mode becomes more questionable here as 
storms may remain a bit more discrete to perhaps remaining in a 
cluster. Or if they can congeal cold pools properly, upscale growth 
into a line is possible. Tough to say which storm mode is correct at 
this time. Aside from capping, sufficient elevated instability will 
be in place with CAPE values up to 1,000 J/kg to 2,000 J/kg with 
effective shear values between 40-50 knots. Thus, damaging winds to 
70 mph and golf ball size hail will be the main hazards. If a storm 
is able to tap into the boundary layer, then an isolated tornado 
will be possible. Especially if the surface warm front can push into 
the forecast area. The storms will push through the area through the 
evening and at least the first half of the overnight hours before 
pushing eastwards with the veering low level jet. 

The daylight hours on Wednesday look to be a quiet as subsidence 
prevails on the backside of the departing wave. Highs will remain 
consistent in the 80s to even low 90s in a few locations. The break 
from rain will be short lived though as another shortwave trough 
will be pushing into the Plains Wednesday night. The ensembles 
support this as they show increasing probabilities up to a 20-50% 
chance for rainfall totals to exceed a tenth of an inch. The 
ensembles have the highest chances for rain east of I-29. Some 
elevated instability looks to be available, suggesting that 
thunderstorms will again be possible. Whether they will be strong to 
severe is uncertain at this time. 

Upper level ridging will be strengthening aloft for the end of this 
week and weekend. High temperatures look to not only remain above 
average but further warm as the ridge becomes more pronounced aloft. 
The ensembles not only support this ridge developing, but also 850 
mb temperatures being pushed to the the 99th percentile of 
climatology. The Euro Extreme Forecast Index (EFI) further supports 
this as it shows 60-80% of its members suggesting above average 
temperatures are possible. Humid conditions look to accompany the 
above average temperatures as the ensembles show a broad 50-90% 
chance for heat indices to exceed 90F. Chances for rain are possible 
(15-30% chance) during this period of time but details are highly 
uncertain. There are some signals that this pattern could begin to 
break down next week. However, medium range guidance continues to 
show increasing variance in this potential. Something to watch to 
see if these conditions will persist into next week.
